paper_title: LIBERO-Industry: Benchmarking Robotic Manipulation under Industrial Process Constraints

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires frequent adaptation to changing products and production conditions, requiring substantial re-engineering effort on conventional automation [Gan et al., 2023, Schlenoff et al., 2021]. Generalist robot policies, including VisionLanguage-Action (VLA) models such as RT-2 [Brohan et al., 2023] and Octo [Ghosh et al., 2024], offer learned alternative by conditioning robot actions on multimodal observations and language instructions across diverse tasks. However, industrial readiness requires more than task-level adaptability, particularly under the precision and operating conditions encountered in industrial settings [Li et al., 2025]. Industrial manipulation in flexible production is shaped by industrial constraints, introducing product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances, as illustrated in Figure 1. Product variants may require different setups and processing times [Gan et al., 2023], making frequent *Corresponding author 1 Figure 1: LIBERO-Industry overview. Motivated by industrial process constraints, the benchmark evaluates generalist robot policies across three classic industrial scenarios. production changes harder to accommodate with fixed systems [Koren et al., 1999]. Moving material flows impose finite time windows for manipulation [Islam et al., 2021], while parts must meet tight geometric tolerances despite manufacturing and perception errors [Jiang et al., 2022]. Traditional automation works reliably when tasks and environments remain stable, but frequent changes often require reprogramming, recalibration, robot re-teaching, or changes to the workcell [Schlenoff et al., 2021, Gan et al., 2023] (detailed in Appendix A, Table 4). Together, these characteristics define the industrial process constraints that embodied manipulation evaluations should capture. However, existing embodied-manipulation and manufacturing-oriented benchmarks do not systematically evaluate generalist robot policy performance under industrial constraints, as summarized in Table 1. On one hand, general-purpose manipulation benchmarks, such as LIBERO, CALVIN, and Meta-World, provide standardized protocols for studying task learning, generalization, and language-conditioned control [Liu et al., 2023, Mees et al., 2022, Yu et al., 2019], yet largely abstract away the timing, motion, and placement requirements imposed by production processes. On the other hand, manufacturing-oriented research and benchmarks, including the Agile Robotics for Industrial Automation Competition (ARIAC), address robotic flexibility, dynamic production conditions, and operational performance [Harrison et al., 2018, Jiang et al., 2022] but do not comprehensively evaluate these industrial constraints or generalist robot policies. Consequently, how moving sources and destinations, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances affect task success, throughput, and stage-wise failures remains underexplored, particularly as these requirements accumulate across multi-object workloads. To address this research gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, an extension of the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO [Liu et al., 2023] for evaluating generalist robot policies under industrial process constraints, that operationalizes these constraints as controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. As shown in Figure 1, LIBERO-Industry comprises three task suites derived from typical industrial scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. These suites differ in whether workpiece sources and destinations are stationary or moving, capturing different forms of material-flow interaction. Each suite includes three progressive difficulty 2 levels with controlled variations in workspace geometry, visual conditions, and task configuration, together with structured perturbations informed by industrial operating conditions and standards. Tasks couple spatial completion requirements with finite execution windows, allowing process constraints to be introduced systematically and in combination. We evaluate five generalist robot policies, including VLA models and world-action model (WAM) in simulation, measuring task success, throughput, and stage-wise completion. We further assess real-world performance through physical D2S trials on an AUBO-i5H arm, comparing fine-tuning effectiveness with LIBERO-Industry and LIBERO under matched conditions. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: (a) Industrial Process Benchmark: We introduce LIBERO-Industry, novel benchmark that systematically evaluates product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. (b) Process-Constrained Task Design: We translate industrial process requirements as controllable task conditions, including conveyor velocity, bounded execution duration, and geometric completion requirement sizes, enabling their systematic evaluation individually and in combination. (c) Empirical Evaluation and Failure Diagnosis: We benchmark five generalist policies, including VLA models and WAM, showing progressive performance degradation as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.

sections.title: 2.1 Generalist Robot Policies
sections.content: Generalist robot policies map multimodal observations and language instructions to actions across diverse tasks. RT-2 and OpenVLA autoregressively decode discrete action tokens [Brohan et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2024], whereas π0 and π0.5 use flow-matching action heads to generate continuous action chunks [Black et al., 2024, Physical Intelligence, 2025b]. Recent World Action Models (WAMs) couple future-state prediction with action generation. WorldVLA, DreamZero, and Cosmos Policy jointly predict future visual states and actions [Cen et al., 2025, Ye et al., 2026, Kim et al., 2026]. VPP instead conditions action prediction on predictive visual representations; Fast-WAM uses video prediction for co-training but directly decodes actions at inference, while FLARE aligns policy representations with latent embeddings of future observations [Hu et al., 2024, Yuan et al., 2026, Zheng et al., 2025]. However, their behavior under calibrated industrial operating conditions remains underexplored.

sections.title: 2.2 Generalist Robot Manipulation Benchmarks
sections.content: A variety of embodied manipulation benchmarks have been proposed to study multi-task learning, longhorizon control, and knowledge transfer. Meta-World targets multi-task and meta-reinforcement learning, CALVIN evaluates language-conditioned long-horizon execution, and LIBERO studies lifelong knowledge transfer [Yu et al., 2019, Mees et al., 2022, Liu et al., 2023]. This line of work has expanded to robustness under object, scene, viewpoint, physical, and linguistic variations through LIBERO-PRO, LIBEROPLUS, VLA-Arena, and LIBERO-X [Zhou et al., 2025, Fei et al., 2025, Zhang et al., 2025, Wang et al., 3 Table 1: Comparison of recent embodied manipulation and manufacturing-oriented benchmarks across policy and industrial-process evaluation dimensions. denotes explicit evaluation, partial or indirect evaluation, and no evaluation. More recent benchmarks, including DOMINO and the Dynamic Object Manipulation (DOM) benchmark introduced with DynamicVLA, consider dynamic disturbances and moving-object manipulation [Fang et al., 2026, Xie et al., 2026]. Yet these benchmarks do not formulate production-line operating conditions as controllable evaluation variables for generalist policies. LIBERO-Industry addresses this gap through conveyor-driven material flows, finite execution windows, task-specific placement predicates, and repeated multi-object handling, together with process-informed perturbations derived from industrial operating conditions. 2.3 Industrial Process-Aware Evaluation variety of manufacturing-oriented benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate production workflows, industrial manipulation, and robotic logistics. ARIAC assesses robotic agility under changing simulated production orders, AI-CPS evaluates industrial manipulation controllers in Isaac Sim, and RoboBPP studies physics-aware online bin packing using industrial data [National Institute of Standards and Technology, 2025, Zhou et al., 2024, Wang et al., 2025]. Related manufacturing research further characterizes reconfigurability, material transport, cycle-time requirements, and pose accuracy [Gan et al., 2023, Groover, 2014, 4 Monch et al., 2021, International Organization for Standardization, 1998]. Nevertheless, neither embodied manipulation benchmarks nor manufacturing-oriented evaluations systematically assess generalist policies under controlled production-line operating conditions. LIBERO-Industry targets this shared limitation by exposing domain-specific process conditions as controlled benchmark variables across standardized conveyor-transfer tasks.

sections.content: The benchmark aims to evaluate how reliably and efficiently generalist robot policies perform materialtransfer tasks in changing industrial workcells. To support comparable evaluation, each task instance is assigned explicit completion predicates and predeclared episode horizon derived from its transport schedule.

sections.content: Each task has two process-level conditions: transport determines how the source and destination evolve, while temporal opportunity determines when transfer remains feasible. Transport condition. sections.title: 3.4 Task Suites and Difficulty Levels
sections.content: The source and destination transport states produce three non-static transfer suites, summarized in Table 2. Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading: moving source stationary fixture. The policy must acquire continuously transported workpiece before its source opportunity ends and then satisfy the fixturespecific completion predicate. Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading: stationary source intermittently moving destination. The policy must place workpiece during an available destination service period and maintain the required placement as the carrier resumes motion. Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer: moving source intermittently moving destination. The policy must satisfy both the source-acquisition opportunity and the destination-service opportunity before stable placement can be credited. The benchmark instantiates these suites with workpieces from multiple industrial domains and level-specific destination fixtures (for asset inventory see Appendix B.1). For task instance m, the benchmark generator converts the instantiated transport schedule and completion allowance into rollout budget: Troll,m = tstart,m + Tevent,m + Tcomplete,m + tb,m, Kroll,m = fcTroll,m , (5) where tstart,m is the initialization or first-arrival offset, Tevent,m is the time spanned by the relevant transport events, Tcomplete,m is the final manipulation or service allowance, and tb,m is the terminal buffer. Appendix B.4 expands this expression for D2S, S2D, and D2D and reports the fixed allowances for every suite, level, and transport condition. These values are shared by all evaluated policies and are benchmark time limits rather than universal factory takt times. Each level preserves the same high-level transfer objective while jointly increasing completion precision and environmental variation: Level 1 pairs broad tray region with the nominal workcell condition, Level 2 adds object-matched grooves with prescribed orientations and bounded perturbations, and Level 3 combines form-fitting inlays with broader perturbations. For moving destinations, success additionally requires carrier retention during transport, with perturbations specified using the pose-accuracy and pose-repeatability terminology of ISO 9283 [International Organization for Standardization, 1998] (see Secs. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Following the experimental setup (Section 4.1), we evaluate overall benchmark performance (Section 4.2), analyze how performance changes as industrial stressors accumulate and where failures concentrate (Section 4.3), and assess whether co-training with LIBERO-Industry simulation data improves physical D2S performance and robustness over co-training with the original LIBERO data (Section 4.4).

sections.content: Table 3 reports performance across the 36 held-out tasks. All five checkpoints were evaluated over 360 rollouts. None satisfied the complete-task success predicate, yielding an SR of 0.0% (0/360) for every policy. The suite-level breakdown likewise shows zero SR in S2D, D2S, and D2D (details in Appendix C.2). Among the evaluated policies, π0.5 exhibits the strongest observed partial-completion profile. It is the only policy with nonzero target-transfer completion (PCRT = 0.4% overall, including 1.1% in S2D) and also records the highest terminal-slot occupancy (PCRS = 12.5%, compared with 11.212.2% for the remaining policies). The held-out BDDL specifications yield mean initial-state slotting baseline of PCRinit = 12.31% (12.3% at the reporting precision of Table 3; see Appendix C.2). Thus, PCRS values near this baseline largely reflect pre-existing destination workpieces that remain valid, whereas newly completed target transfers are isolated by PCRT.

sections.title: 4.3 Ablation and Findings
sections.content: Figure 3 traces the cumulative D0D6 stress progression for π0.5. SR declines from 97.0% at D0 to 43.8% at D4, then collapses to 2.1% at D5 and 0.0% at D6 as the task expands from one to multiple objects. Because each stage retains the preceding modifications, the progression is diagnostic rather than causal. Partial transfer persists at D5D6 (PCRT = 18.1% and 11.5%), while reach-stage failures account for 132/240 and 202/240 episodes, respectively, localizing the principal bottleneck to longer multi-object sequences (Appendix C.3; Appendix C.3.3).

sections.title: 4.4 Real-World Experiments
sections.content: We evaluate held-out physical D2S unloading on an AUBOi5HCTAG2F90D workcell. Each trial requires the policy to transfer three workpieces sequentially from moving conveyor into stationary Level 1 tray. The evaluation uses four three-workpiece combinations and two held-out slot permutations per combination, yielding eight held-out object-order configurations. At each conveyor speed, each policy is evaluated over 24 trials, corresponding to 72 planned placements per policyspeed condition. The held-out combinations and permutations are disjoint from the physical training split (Appendix E.2; Table 18). We compare two simreal co-training setups initialized from the same π0.5 base checkpoint. S1 combines 1,724 original-LIBERO simulation demonstrations with 95 physical D2S demonstrations, whereas S2 combines 1,412 LIBERO-Industry simulation demonstrations with the same 95 physical demonstrations. Both use the same 9:1 frame-based simulation-to-real sampling ratio, 30,000 training steps, model configuration, and physical evaluation protocol. The comparison therefore isolates the simulation-data source and corpus size while holding the physical supervision and training procedure fixed (Appendix E.4; Table 20). 9 Figure 3: Cumulative diagnostic stress progression for π0.5. Each bar denotes complete-task success of the stress settings for trials (D0D1: = 200; D2D6: = 240), and PCRT denotes mean targetobject transfer completion. Stars show mean policy steps over successful trajectories; D6 has no successful trajectories. The progression is diagnostic rather than causal. Figure 4B reports target-transfer completion at conveyor speeds of 0.03 and 0.05 m/s. At 0.03 m/s, S2 achieves PCRT = 34.7% (25/72), compared with 26.4% (19/72) for S1; at 0.05 m/s, the corresponding values are 23.6% (17/72) and 4.2% (3/72). The fraction of trials completing the third placement is also higher for S2: 16.7% versus 4.2% at 0.03 m/s and 20.8% versus 0.0% at 0.05 m/s. Across both aggregate transfer completion and later placement steps, S2 maintains higher observed performance, with the largest separation at the faster conveyor speed. Figure 4C evaluates changes in illumination, object appearance, camera configuration, and table texture. S2 exceeds S1 across all five evaluated variations by 12.534.7 percentage points, with the largest difference under the camera variation (34.7% versus 0.0%). This consistent ordering indicates that the observed advantage of S2 extends beyond the nominal D2S configuration under the tested physical operating-condition changes.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion and future work
sections.content: We introduced LIBERO-Industry, benchmark for evaluating generalist policies under industrial process constraints, including product variability, material flows, finite execution-time windows, and tight geometric tolerance. Built on LIBERO, the benchmark organizes these conditions into S2D , D2S and D2D task 10 Figure 4: Real-world validation. A: AUBOi5HCTAG2F90D D2S workcell. B: Per-step release-on-tray success for S1 and S2 at conveyor speeds of 0.03 and 0.05 m/s over 24 trials per condition; the table reports aggregate target-transfer completion as PCRT out of 72 planned placements. C: Target-transfer completion (PCRT) under five physical operating-condition variations, with exact values labeled. suites, with controlled variations in task configuration and operating conditions. Our results show performance degradation across the cumulative industrial stress progression and higher D2S manipulation ability and generalization for the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition than for the original-LIBERO condition. key future direction is to determine whether generalist policies can retain flexibility without sacrificing industrial production rates; the benchmarks finite opportunity windows abstract this requirement from heterogeneous factory needs. Future evaluation should move toward production-calibrated settings that relate cycle times to empirical operating rates and test repeated material arrivals, recovery events, and long-horizon throughput. Ultimately, industrial readiness should be assessed not only by task completion but by compatibility with diverse production processes.

sections.title: A Control Paradigms and Technical Comparison
sections.content: This section provides structured comparison of traditional, learning-based, and generalist robotic control paradigms. Table 4 outlines the trade-offs in model scale, data dependencies, and physical precision limits that motivate the transition toward high-fidelity simulation environments like LIBERO-Industry. Table 4: Comparative Analysis of Control Paradigms in Industrial Manipulation Tasks. Paradigm Representative Arch. / Algos Model Size & Freq. Traditional Rule-Driven Modular PerceptionAction FSM / BT; A* / TAMP; PID, Force, Hybrid PositionForce, Impedance YOLOv8 / FastSAM + LLM-TAMP (MoveIt / OMPL) Imitation Learning (IL) ACT, Diffusion Policy, DP3 Model-Free / Residual RL PPO, SAC, OEC-IRRL, RLGeneralist Robot Policies VLA models: RT-2, OpenVLA; generalist diffusion/transformer policies: Octo, RDT-1B No learned params; 1000 2000 Hz Perception: 100M1B+ (< 10 Hz); Planner: Det. (> 200 Hz) 50M100M params; 30100 Hz inference < 20M params; > 500 Hz 1B7B+ params; 310 Hz World Action Models (WAM) DreamZero, 1XWM, UniSim 14B+ params; 37 Hz closed-loop control Data / Training Source Zero data; physical models & expert kinematics Zero downstream trajectories; pre-trained vision & 3D CAD models Behavioral cloning from 50100 expert demonstrations Online/Offline RL via environment reward signals Multi-task or multiembodiment pre-training with language, image-goal, or action conditioning Joint video-action diffusion / latent generative dynamics Typical Precision & Repeatability Typically sub-millimeter repeatability in calibrated industrial setups Reported millimeter-scale alignment, depending on perception and calibration Sub-millimeter performance reported for structured task-specific settings Taskand reward-dependent; sub-millimeter alignment reported in selected settings Centimeter-scale errors reported in selected precision-placement evaluations Task-dependent; no standardized physical-repeatability measure Precision and repeatability summarize representative reported results and depend on the robot, sensing and calibration pipeline, task geometry, and evaluation protocol. As detailed in Table 4, the landscape of robotic manipulation control can be broadly categorized into distinct evolutionary tiers, each exhibiting specific deployment bottlenecks when transitioned to High-Mix LowVolume (HMLV) manufacturing: 17 1. Classical and Modular Control Stacks. Classical robot systems separate task sequencing, motion planning, trajectory generation, and feedback control. Finite-state machines and behavior trees encode process logic, while geometric or task-and-motion planners generate feasible motions. PID, force, hybrid positionforce, and impedance controllers then regulate trajectory tracking and physical interaction [Garrett et al., 2021, Whitney, 1977, Raibert and Craig, 1981, Hogan, 1985]. These systems can provide high-rate feedback and repeatable execution under calibrated conditions, but their performance depends on accurate models, engineered task logic, and careful integration of perception, planning, and control. 2. Task-Specific Learning Policies. Imitation Learning methods such as ACT and Diffusion Policy learn observation-to-action mappings from expert demonstrations, whereas model-free Reinforcement Learning optimizes behavior through task-specific reward signals [Zhao et al., 2023, Chi et al., 2023, Haarnoja et al., 2018]. These approaches reduce the need to manually specify every motion or contact strategy and can represent temporally coordinated or multimodal behaviors. However, their performance remains closely tied to the training task, embodiment, observationaction interface, reward design, and coverage of demonstrations or environment interactions. 3. Generalist Robot Policies and World Action Models. Generalist robot policies use multi-task or multi-embodiment pretraining to support language-conditioned behavior and transfer across tasks. VLAs such as RT-2 and OpenVLA directly connect visual and language inputs to robot actions, while Octo and RDT-1B use generalist transformer or diffusion-policy formulations [Brohan et al., 2023, Kim et al., 2024]. World Action Models additionally predict future visual dynamics together with action sequences, providing an explicit generative representation of how the scene may evolve [Ye et al., 2026]. Their broader semantic and task coverage is promising, although runtime frequency, contact behavior, and physical precision continue to depend on the model architecture, inference hardware, action representation, and downstream adaptation.

Columns progress from Level 1 sector trays to Level 2 object-specific grooves and Level 3 form-fitting inlays. Header and border colors identify difficulty levels and do not encode measured performance. We introduce collection of industrial object assets spanning several manufacturing domains. The base models are adapted from publicly accessible and commercial asset repositories, including an industrial conveyor model [Lovano, 2023], Google Scanned Objects [Downs et al., 2022], and commercial design configurations [ProductViz3D, 2025].
